Connections can transmit mistakes as well as discoveries. Access, incentives, trust, and institutions affect whether useful knowledge survives.

The lesson is to build learning pathways, not simply bigger crowds.

slides.title: Leave a better starting point
slides.html:
On your next project, ask three questions: What did I inherit? Whose different expertise could improve it? What should I record so someone else can build on it?

Even a concise note, reusable method, or documented failure can be a contribution to a collective brain.

title: A smaller AI can learn from a bigger one's mistakes
kicker: Why the wrong answers can teach more than the right one
hook: A teacher says 'cat.' A better teacher says 'cat, but it looks a little like a fox.'
author: Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals and Jeff Dean
source_title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
summary: Knowledge distillation trains a compact student network to match a larger teacher's softened output probabilities, not just the correct label. The pattern of less likely alternatives carries information about similarities between classes. The paper reports results on handwritten-digit recognition and speech recognition; success depends on the teacher, student and task.
body: A standard classifier often learns from a single correct class. That label hides what else the example resembles.
Distillation uses a trained teacher's probability distribution as an additional learning signal. A temperature adjustment exposes relationships among unlikely alternatives.
The authors demonstrated the approach on MNIST and an acoustic speech-recognition model, showing that a smaller deployable model can benefit from a larger ensemble's predictions.
takeaways: A teacher's uncertainty can carry useful structure about similarities.
A smaller student can learn from a teacher's outputs without copying its architecture or weights.
Training-time compute and deployment-time compute need not be the same.
nuance: The paper does not show that any small model can perfectly reproduce any large model. Soft labels can also transmit teacher errors, and the paper's empirical evidence is task-specific.
application: When building a compact classifier, consider training it against a stronger teacher's softened predictions and evaluating it independently on held-out examples.

quiz.question: What extra information can a teacher's softened predictions give a student?
choices: Which incorrect classes resemble the example
The teacher's exact internal weights
A guarantee that the student will never err
quiz.explanation: Relative probabilities of alternatives reveal learned similarities, though they may also reflect teacher errors.

slides.title: What can a wrong answer teach?
slides.html:
A picture is labeled cat. That tells a model what it is, but not what it almost looks like.

Imagine a teacher adding: it is much more like a fox than a bicycle. Those near-misses can be useful information.

Can a small AI learn from a larger AI's entire pattern of guesses?

slides.title: A label versus a lesson
slides.html:
Traditional labels identify the correct class. A trained teacher offers a distribution across classes: which alternatives look plausible, and which are absurd.

The numbers below are illustrative, not measurements from the paper.

left.label: HARD LABEL
left.title: Cat
left.text: Cat: yes. Fox: no. Bicycle: no.

right.label: SOFT TEACHER
right.title: Cat, with context
right.text: Cat: likely. Fox: somewhat similar. Bicycle: extremely unlikely.

slides.title: Turn up the temperature
slides.html:
A confident teacher may assign almost all probability to one answer. The useful differences between the alternatives become tiny.

Hinton and colleagues used a temperature setting to soften the probabilities. The student learns to match this softened pattern, often alongside the real labels.

No one needs to copy the teacher's internal weights.

slides.title: Big teacher, small student
slides.html: The expensive teacher can be trained offline. The smaller student learns from its predictions and is the model eventually deployed.

items.title: Train teacher
items.text: Build a strong model or ensemble.

items.title: Produce soft targets
items.text: Reveal how the teacher ranks possible answers.

items.title: Train student
items.text: Match those targets in a smaller network.

slides.title: Did it actually help?
slides.html:
The 2015 paper studied handwritten-digit recognition and acoustic speech recognition. The authors reported useful results from transferring an ensemble's behavior into a smaller model, including improvements in a commercial speech system.

That supports distillation as a practical technique in those settings. It does not prove every tiny model can absorb everything a larger one knows.

slides.title: Which teacher is more informative?
slides.html: Two teachers correctly identify a handwritten 3. One only reports the answer. The other also reveals that it resembles an 8 more than a 1.

interaction.prompt: Which teacher gives a small student more information?
interaction.answer: The second: its relative probabilities describe a similarity structure. But if its judgments are unreliable, the student can inherit those mistakes.

title: The best way to scale may be to start manually
kicker: A counterintuitive lesson from early startups
hook: What if doing work by hand is the fastest way to discover what software should automate?
author: Paul Graham
source_title: Do Things that Don't Scale
summary: Paul Graham argues that early startups often need deliberately manual efforts: recruiting users individually, helping them personally, and even performing a service by hand before automating it. Such work can generate the feedback needed to discover what to build, though the essay is founder advice supported by examples rather than controlled evidence.
body: An early product may not attract users by itself. Graham argues that founders often must recruit users personally and offer unusually attentive support.
Some founders can deliver a service manually before building automation, discovering the actual workflow and bottlenecks through experience.
The approach should change as demand grows; the goal is learning what is worth scaling, not permanently hiding manual labor.
takeaways: Manual service can be a research tool, not merely a workaround.
A handful of engaged users may teach more than a large but indifferent audience.
Automate observed bottlenecks rather than imagined ones.
nuance: This is an influential entrepreneurial argument built on case examples, not a randomized test or universal law. Manual service can mask weak demand or create unsustainable expectations; safety-critical and regulated services require additional care.
application: For a new product idea, serve three prospective users personally, note repeated steps and points of friction, and automate only what repeats.

quiz.question: Why might a founder initially deliver a service manually?
choices: To avoid ever writing software
To discover real user needs and recurring steps before automating
Because all successful products must stay manual
quiz.explanation: Hands-on delivery exposes what users value and which parts of the process deserve automation.

slides.title: Your first product might be a person
slides.html:
Suppose you want to build software that plans weekend trips. You could spend months creating a recommendation engine.

Or you could plan ten trips manually for real people and notice which parts they love, ignore, or change.

The second approach sounds less scalable. It might teach you more.

slides.title: Don't automate a guess
slides.html:
In his 2013 essay, Paul Graham argues that young startups often need to do things that large companies cannot afford to do: recruit users one by one, personally solve problems, and offer exceptional attention.

That isn't just marketing. It can be a way to learn what the product should become.

slides.title: Build first or learn first?
slides.html: Automation is powerful when you know which task matters. Before that, it can make the wrong process faster.

left.label: AUTOMATE EARLY
left.title: Scale assumptions
left.text: Build a complete workflow before observing many users.

right.label: SERVE MANUALLY
right.title: Find the real bottleneck
right.text: Solve the problem directly, observe friction, then automate repeated steps.

slides.title: The founders who carried laptops
slides.html:
Graham recounts how the early Stripe team did not simply email interested users a signup link. They helped people get set up immediately, sometimes taking their laptops and doing the installation.

He also describes founders handling work behind the scenes before automating it. These are illustrative startup stories, not controlled comparisons.

slides.title: Which part would you automate?
slides.html: You manually create five trip itineraries. Each person wants different destinations, but all five ask for an easy way to compare travel times.

interaction.prompt: What should you build first?
interaction.answer: A travel-time comparison tool is a promising first feature: it addresses repeated observed friction. Test whether users actually value it before expanding.

slides.title: Manual isn't always better
slides.html:
Graham's essay is practical advice, not proof that every startup should use this approach.

Personal service can hide weak demand, become costly, or set expectations you cannot maintain. The useful question is not whether manual work can scale forever.

It is whether manual work helps you discover what deserves to scale.

title: The people who didn't get sick cracked the case
kicker: A Victorian detective story about causal evidence
hook: Why did a brewery escape a deadly outbreak in the middle of London?
author: John Snow
source_title: On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (second edition)
summary: During London's 1854 cholera outbreak, physician John Snow investigated not only the concentration of deaths near a public pump but also exceptions to that pattern. Differences in water consumption helped distinguish his waterborne explanation from the prevailing bad-air theory.
body: Snow mapped deaths and investigated where people obtained drinking water.
A nearby brewery escaped severe illness among its workers, who did not use the implicated street pump. A woman living far away who had its water delivered died of cholera.
The pump handle was removed, but the outbreak was already declining, making the intervention alone insufficient to establish its effect.
takeaways: Exceptions can distinguish competing explanations.
Measure exposure rather than assuming proximity is exposure.
A decline after an intervention does not necessarily establish causation.
nuance: Snow's investigation was observational, not randomized. He did not establish the precise effect of removing the pump handle; his evidence came from multiple comparisons and investigations.
application: When investigating a failure, compare affected cases with nearby unaffected cases and distant affected cases. Ask what exposure they actually share.

quiz.question: Why was the brewery especially informative?
choices: It was far from the outbreak
Its workers shared the neighborhood but avoided the suspected water source
It proved beer cures cholera
quiz.explanation: The contrast helped separate geographic proximity from actual exposure to the pump water.

slides.title: A mystery on Broad Street
slides.html:
London, 1854. Cholera is killing people in a crowded neighborhood. Many blame foul air. Physician John Snow suspects drinking water instead.

His most revealing clues include people who stayed healthy right beside the outbreak, and people who fell ill far away.

slides.title: A map is only the beginning
slides.html:
Snow recorded where victims lived or became ill and marked deaths on a map alongside public pumps.

Many clustered around the Broad Street pump. But geography alone could not settle the argument: people living nearby shared both air and access to water.

slides.title: Same neighborhood, different exposure
slides.html: Snow investigated groups that did not fit the simple geographic pattern.

left.label: NEAR THE PUMP
left.title: Brewery workers
left.text: Their employer reported no severe cholera among the workers, who did not use the street pump.

right.label: FAR AWAY
right.title: A woman in Hampstead
right.text: She had Broad Street water delivered and died after drinking it.

slides.title: What would you investigate next?
slides.html: Imagine two adjacent buildings. One has many cases; the other has almost none. Both breathe the same neighborhood air.

interaction.prompt: What difference would you look for?
interaction.answer: Compare their water sources and actual drinking habits. The contrasting exposures can help distinguish explanations that a map alone cannot separate.

slides.title: The handle is not the whole story
slides.html:
Officials removed the pump handle on September 8. But new cases were already falling. Snow himself acknowledged that the effect of the removal was uncertain.

The stronger lesson is to combine independent clues, especially exceptions that competing explanations struggle to explain.

title: A price can carry news without telling the story
hook: How can a factory react to a shortage it has never heard about?
author: Friedrich A. Hayek
source_title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
summary: Hayek's 1945 essay argues that changing prices can communicate scarcity across a network of buyers and sellers without requiring each participant to know the underlying events. His example of tin illustrates how decentralized adjustments can coordinate resource use.
body: Relevant economic knowledge is distributed across people and places.
A change in the price of tin can encourage users to conserve it or find substitutes without knowing why it became scarce.
Prices communicate some information but do not automatically capture every social cost or guarantee fair outcomes.
takeaways: A signal can coordinate action without explaining its cause.
Local knowledge matters when circumstances change.
Useful signals are not necessarily complete measures of social value.
nuance: This is a theoretical argument, not an empirical demonstration that markets always allocate resources efficiently. Market power, externalities and unequal purchasing power can distort outcomes.
application: When designing a shared resource system, ask which local signals would help users adjust their behavior and which important costs those signals would omit.

quiz.question: What does Hayek's tin example illustrate?
choices: Everyone must know why a shortage happened
A price change can coordinate responses without everyone knowing the cause
Prices always measure social welfare perfectly
quiz.explanation: The price transmits actionable information about relative scarcity without transmitting the entire underlying story.

slides.title: The factory that never heard the news
slides.html:
Imagine a factory using tin. Somewhere overseas, a mine closes. The factory manager never reads about it.

Yet the factory starts using less tin. How could information about a distant event change a local decision without anyone explaining what happened?

slides.title: Nobody sees the whole economy
slides.html:
In his 1945 essay, economist Friedrich Hayek emphasizes that practical knowledge is scattered among people. A supplier knows its inventory; a buyer knows which materials it can replace.

Coordinating their decisions is not just a calculation problem. It is also a communication problem.

slides.title: From shortage to substitution
slides.html: Hayek uses tin as a hypothetical example of how a price can transmit information.

items.label: EVENT
items.title: Tin becomes scarcer
items.text: Supply falls or another use becomes more valuable.

items.label: RESPONSE
items.title: Users adapt
items.text: Some conserve tin or switch to alternatives.

slides.title: A signal is not the whole truth
slides.html:
A price may reflect scarcity without reflecting pollution, unequal access, or the consequences for people who cannot afford a product.

Hayek offers an argument about coordination, not proof that every market outcome is desirable. A useful signal can still leave out information that matters.

slides.title: Design a better signal
slides.html: Imagine several teams sharing limited computing capacity. Each team knows which jobs are urgent, but no central manager knows every detail.

interaction.prompt: What could help teams coordinate?
interaction.answer: A visible congestion or resource-cost signal could encourage flexible jobs to move. Critical jobs may still need reserved capacity or explicit priority rules.

title: You might defend a choice you never made
hook: What if someone secretly swapped your decision—and you explained why you made it?
author: Petter Johansson, Lars Hall, Sverker Sikström and Andreas Olsson
source_title: Failure to Detect Mismatches Between Intention and Outcome in a Simple Decision Task
summary: In a 2005 experiment, people selected the more attractive of two faces. Researchers sometimes used a trick to show them the unchosen face as though it were their choice. Some participants failed to notice and supplied reasons for the switched outcome, illustrating limits of introspection about decisions.
body: Participants chose between two photographed faces. On some trials, the experimenter secretly substituted the unchosen photograph.
Some participants did not detect the substitution and explained why they preferred the face they were shown.
This is evidence that explanations can sometimes be constructed after an outcome, not proof that all preferences are arbitrary.
takeaways: An articulate explanation is not always a faithful record of the original decision.
Check whether a reported choice matches what was actually selected.
Choice blindness is demonstrated in particular experimental settings, not every decision.
nuance: The experimental manipulation involved simple attractiveness judgments. It does not show that people routinely fail to notice major real-world reversals or that all reasons are invented.
application: When reviewing an important decision, write down the choice and reasoning before seeing the outcome; compare the record with later explanations.

quiz.question: What was the key experimental manipulation?
choices: Changing participants' memories with medication
Presenting the unchosen face as if it had been selected
Asking people to choose without seeing any faces
quiz.explanation: The researchers covertly switched the outcome of some choices and observed whether people detected the mismatch.

slides.title: Explain the choice you didn't make
slides.html:
You choose one of two faces. The experimenter hands you the photograph you supposedly preferred and asks why.

You give a convincing explanation. But there's a catch: the photograph was secretly switched. You are explaining a choice you never made.

slides.title: A simple switch
slides.html:
In a 2005 study, Johansson and colleagues asked participants to select the more attractive face from pairs of photographs.

On some trials, a sleight-of-hand manipulation substituted the face they had not chosen. The researchers watched for detection and asked participants to explain their supposed preference.

slides.title: Two different histories
slides.html: The crucial distinction is between what the participant selected and what they were subsequently shown.

left.label: ACTUAL CHOICE
left.title: Face A
left.text: The participant points to A.

right.label: SWITCHED OUTCOME
right.title: Face B
right.text: The experimenter presents B as the chosen face.

slides.title: A reason is not a recording
slides.html:
Some participants failed to notice the mismatch. They still offered reasons for preferring the substituted face.

The researchers called this choice blindness. It suggests that our explanations can sometimes be constructed around the outcome we believe we chose.

slides.title: How would you test your own reasons?
slides.html: Suppose you are choosing between two job offers. Months later, you confidently explain why your decision was inevitable.

interaction.prompt: What record could help distinguish original reasons from hindsight?
interaction.answer: Write down your preferred option and the reasons before accepting an offer. Later, compare the original record with the story you now tell.

slides.title: Not every choice is blind
slides.html:
The study used a specific, relatively simple judgment and a covert substitution. It does not mean people never know their own preferences or would overlook every important reversal.

Its useful warning is narrower: confidence in an explanation is not proof that it accurately reconstructs a decision.

title: Teach a computer to see with captions instead of labels
hook: What if recognizing new objects did not require training a new classifier for each category?
author: Alec Radford and colleagues
source_title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
summary: CLIP trains image and text encoders to identify which caption belongs with which image across a large collection of image–text pairs. At inference, it compares a new image against text descriptions of candidate categories, enabling zero-shot classification on many benchmarks without task-specific training.
body: Conventional image classifiers often rely on a fixed set of manually labeled categories. CLIP instead learns from paired images and natural-language text.
Its training objective brings matching image and caption representations closer while distinguishing mismatched pairs.
The authors trained on 400 million image–text pairs and evaluated transfer on more than 30 datasets, finding substantial zero-shot capabilities but uneven performance.
takeaways: Natural-language captions can provide flexible supervision for visual recognition.
Contrastive learning aligns two different kinds of inputs in a shared representation space.
Zero-shot transfer means no task-specific training at evaluation, not no training at all.
nuance: The model required a huge pretraining dataset and compute. Its performance varies by task and distribution, and web-sourced data can carry biases. The paper does not establish reliable understanding of every image or prompt.
application: For a small visual classification prototype, compare descriptions such as 'a photo of a bicycle' and 'a photo of a scooter' rather than assuming every class needs a new supervised training run; validate on representative data.

quiz.question: How can CLIP classify a category without training a new task-specific head?
choices: It compares image representations with text descriptions of candidate categories
It searches the web for every new image
It memorizes every possible class name during evaluation
quiz.explanation: CLIP learns a shared image–text space, so candidate class descriptions can be compared directly with an image.

slides.title: What if pictures learned from words?
slides.html:
Imagine teaching a computer to recognize a skateboard, a flamingo, or a traffic cone.

Traditionally, you might collect labeled examples for every category. CLIP asks a different question: can an AI learn useful visual concepts simply by matching pictures with the text people write about them?

slides.title: Find the matching caption
slides.html:
During training, CLIP sees batches of pictures and captions. Two encoders convert images and text into representations that can be compared.

The objective rewards the true image–caption pairs over mismatched combinations.

items.label: INPUT
items.title: Image and caption
items.text: A photo of a dog beside a bicycle.

items.label: ENCODE
items.title: Two representations
items.text: An image encoder and a text encoder produce comparable vectors.

items.label: LEARN
items.title: Match the right pair
items.text: Increase similarity for matching pairs relative to mismatches.

slides.title: New labels can be sentences
slides.html:
After training, CLIP can compare a new image with text prompts such as 'a photo of a cat' and 'a photo of a dog.'

The closest match becomes its prediction. That is called zero-shot classification: the model needs no additional training specifically on that classification dataset.

slides.title: A large experiment, not a magic trick
slides.html:
The authors trained with 400 million image–text pairs and evaluated transfer on more than 30 existing vision datasets.

They reported that a zero-shot CLIP model matched the original ResNet-50's ImageNet accuracy without training on ImageNet's labeled training set. Results varied across tasks.

slides.title: What does zero-shot actually mean?
slides.html: A CLIP model is asked to distinguish a bicycle from a scooter using those two words as candidate labels.

interaction.prompt: Has the model learned without examples?
interaction.answer: No. It has already learned from a very large collection of image–text pairs. Zero-shot means it does not need additional labeled training examples for this specific evaluation task.

slides.title: Captions aren't perfect teachers
slides.html:
Web captions can be incomplete, misleading, or biased. Training on hundreds of millions of pairs also requires substantial resources.

CLIP demonstrated a flexible route to visual recognition, not perfect visual understanding or dependable performance in every setting. The enduring idea is learning a reusable connection between language and images.

title: A walk helps you invent ideas—not necessarily solve them
hook: Why might pacing help you brainstorm but not find the one correct answer?
author: Marily Oppezzo and Daniel L. Schwartz
source_title: Give Your Ideas Some Legs: The Positive Effect of Walking on Creative Thinking
summary: Four experiments found that walking improved generation of novel possibilities, including indoors on a treadmill, but did not similarly improve a focused word-association task.
body: The researchers compared people sitting and walking while completing tasks that required either many possible answers or one correct answer.

Walking generally improved divergent idea generation, and some benefit persisted briefly after participants sat down. Outdoor stimulation alone did not explain the result: treadmill walking also helped.
The distinction matters: walking can be a useful way to open up possibilities, not a universal boost to every kind of thinking.
takeaways: Match your thinking environment to the cognitive task.
Try walking when generating options, metaphors or alternative approaches.
Return to focused evaluation when you need to select or verify a solution.
nuance: The four experiments involved 176 mostly college-aged participants and short laboratory tasks. They do not establish the mechanism, long-term productivity gains, or that walking improves all reasoning.
application: Take a short walk while generating five alternative solutions to a problem. Then sit down to test and rank them.

quiz.question: Which task was most consistently helped by walking in these experiments?
choices: Generating multiple unusual uses for an object
Finding one correct word association
Every form of analytical reasoning
quiz.explanation: Walking benefited divergent idea generation, while the tested convergent word-association task did not show the same benefit.

slides.title: Why do ideas arrive when you walk?
slides.html:
Imagine being stuck at your desk. You get up, pace for a few minutes, and suddenly have three new approaches.

Is that just a pleasant feeling—or does walking actually change the kinds of ideas you generate?

slides.title: Many possibilities versus one answer
slides.html: Oppezzo and Schwartz tested two distinct cognitive tasks. The distinction turned out to matter more than a generic claim that exercise makes us smarter.

left.label: DIVERGENT
left.title: Generate possibilities
left.text: Think of unusual uses for a common object.

right.label: CONVERGENT
right.title: Find one solution
right.text: Find a word that connects three given words.

slides.title: Walking opened up the option space
slides.html:
Across four experiments, walking improved performance on tasks involving novel uses and analogies. The effect appeared on a treadmill as well as outdoors, and sometimes lingered after people sat down.

But walking did not improve the tested single-answer word-association task in the same way.

slides.title: It wasn't simply the scenery
slides.html: One experiment separated moving your body from seeing an outdoor environment. Participants walked outside, walked on a treadmill, sat indoors, or were pushed outside in a wheelchair.

items.title: Score ideas
items.text: Evaluate novelty and quality of analogies.

slides.title: Which problem would you take on a walk?
slides.html: You have two tasks: brainstorm ten ways to reuse an empty jar, or verify the arithmetic in a tax calculation.

interaction.prompt: Which one matches the strongest experimental evidence?
interaction.answer: Brainstorming alternative uses. The studies support a benefit for generating possibilities, not a blanket improvement in exact-answer tasks.

slides.title: A creativity tool, not a universal brain upgrade
slides.html:
The experiments were brief and mostly involved college-aged adults. They did not establish why walking helps, or prove that a walking meeting improves every real-world decision.

Practical experiment: walk to generate options; sit to evaluate them.

title: To see life's machinery, freeze water without making ice
kicker: The strange trick behind a microscopy revolution
hook: How do you photograph a fragile molecule when the microscope itself can destroy it?
author: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
source_title: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2017 — Press Release
summary: Cryo-electron microscopy made fragile biological molecules far easier to study by combining rapid cooling that traps water in a glass-like state, low-dose electron imaging, and computational reconstruction from many noisy views. The 2017 Chemistry Nobel recognized three scientists whose complementary advances helped make this possible.
body: Electron microscopes can reveal extremely small structures, but their vacuum and powerful electron beam create serious problems for water-rich, fragile biological samples.

Jacques Dubochet developed rapid cooling that vitrifies water instead of forming damaging ice crystals. Joachim Frank developed methods for combining fuzzy two-dimensional views into three-dimensional structures. Richard Henderson demonstrated that high-resolution electron imaging of proteins was possible.
These advances, together with subsequent improvements in detectors and methods, transformed structural biology. They do not make every molecule easy to image or eliminate sample damage.
takeaways: Preserving a specimen can be as important as improving the instrument.
Many noisy views can yield a detailed three-dimensional reconstruction when processed appropriately.
Breakthroughs often require several complementary inventions rather than a single eureka moment.
nuance: Cryo-EM reconstructs structures from many molecular images rather than directly filming a single molecule at atomic detail. Resolution varies by specimen, preparation and instrumentation. The Nobel account summarizes a multi-decade technical history, not one controlled experiment.
application: When a measurement seems impossible, separate the obstacles: preserving the subject, capturing a signal, and reconstructing useful information. Different solutions may be needed for each.

quiz.question: Why does cryo-electron microscopy cool water so rapidly?
choices: To make large ice crystals that magnify molecules
To trap water in a glass-like state that preserves delicate structures
To turn electrons into visible light
quiz.explanation: Rapid cooling vitrifies water, avoiding disruptive ice crystals and helping preserve biomolecules for electron imaging.

slides.title: Freeze water without making ice
slides.html:
Imagine trying to photograph a tiny, delicate machine. The camera needs a vacuum, the machine is surrounded by water, and the beam used to see it can damage it.

How could scientists ever see the machinery inside living cells?

slides.title: The microscope changes what it sees
slides.html:
Electron microscopes can resolve details far smaller than ordinary light microscopes. But biological molecules are fragile.

Water evaporates in a vacuum, ice crystals can distort structures, and electron beams can damage samples. A sharper lens alone cannot solve these problems.

slides.title: Preserve, photograph, reconstruct
slides.html: The breakthrough emerged from complementary advances over decades, recognized by the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

items.label: PRESERVE
items.title: Vitrify the water
items.text: Dubochet's rapid cooling avoids disruptive ice crystals.

items.label: CAPTURE
items.title: Use electrons carefully
items.text: Henderson showed high-resolution protein imaging was possible.

items.label: REBUILD
items.title: Combine noisy views
items.text: Frank developed methods to reconstruct 3D structures from 2D images.

slides.title: Frozen doesn't have to mean crystalline
slides.html:
Normally, freezing water creates ordered ice crystals. Cool it sufficiently fast and it can instead become a glass-like solid, called vitreous ice.

That matters because the molecules can remain embedded in a thin layer of water without large crystals disrupting their arrangement.

slides.title: What makes a fuzzy picture useful?
slides.html: One electron-microscope image of a molecule may be noisy and hard to interpret. Scientists collect many images of particles in different orientations.

interaction.prompt: Why not simply trust the sharpest single picture?
interaction.answer: Computational methods align and combine information across many particle images, helping reconstruct a clearer three-dimensional structure than an individual noisy view provides.

slides.title: Not a magic camera
slides.html:
Cryo-electron microscopy does not directly record a flawless atomic movie of every molecule. Samples can still be damaged, and attainable resolution depends on the specimen and the experiment.

Its larger lesson: sometimes seeing more requires protecting the subject and inventing a better way to combine imperfect observations.

title: The expert's secret weapon is a tiny checklist
hook: What if the hardest failures happen not because we don't know what to do, but because we forget one crucial step?
author: Atul Gawande
source_title: The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right
summary: In complex work, expertise can coexist with preventable omissions. Gawande shows why a brief checklist can support skilled teams without replacing judgment.
body: Modern surgery depends on immense specialist knowledge. Yet knowing the right steps is not the same as reliably completing every step under pressure.
Atul Gawande argues that a well-designed checklist protects a small number of critical actions, especially when work involves many people and interruptions.
The point is not to turn professionals into robots. It is to free their attention for the difficult decisions by making routine essentials harder to miss.
takeaways: Identify the few omissions that would cause disproportionate harm.
Use a short pause at the moment those steps matter.
Treat a checklist as a coordination tool, not a substitute for expertise.
nuance: The book describes successes in aviation and medicine, but not every checklist improves outcomes. Adoption, team culture, and selecting the right steps matter.
application: Before your next complicated release or trip, list five easily forgotten, high-consequence checks. Run them at the actual handoff point.

quiz.question: What problem is a well-designed checklist primarily trying to solve?
choices: A lack of expert knowledge
Critical steps being missed amid complexity
The need to eliminate professional judgment
quiz.explanation: Checklists make essential actions more reliable while leaving complex decisions to skilled people.

slides.title: Knowing isn't always doing
slides.html:
Imagine a surgical team with years of training. Everyone knows that a particular safety step matters. Yet in a busy operating room, it can still be missed.

The failure isn't necessarily ignorance. It may be complexity overwhelming reliable execution.

slides.title: Experts need memory outside their heads
slides.html:
In The Checklist Manifesto, surgeon Atul Gawande explores how specialists can know an extraordinary amount and still overlook a basic action.

A checklist is a small external memory designed for the moments when attention is scarce and the cost of omission is high.

slides.title: Don't checklist the judgment
slides.html: The useful distinction is between critical repeatable steps and decisions that require interpretation. A checklist supports the former so experts can focus on the latter.

left.label: CHECK
left.title: Did we do it?
left.text: Confirm a critical action at the right moment.

right.label: JUDGE
right.title: What should we do?
right.text: Use expertise to interpret an unfamiliar situation.

slides.title: Where would a checklist help?
slides.html: A software team repeatedly forgets to check a deployment rollback path. Which intervention fits the book's argument best?

interaction.question: Choose the most useful response.
choices: Tell everyone to concentrate harder
Add a short pre-release check for rollback readiness
Replace the team's technical judgment with a 40-page script
interaction.feedback: A brief, timely check targets a recurring omission without pretending every release decision is routine.

slides.title: A checklist can become noise
slides.html:
More boxes do not automatically mean more safety. A sprawling checklist can distract, and a team that treats it as ceremony may ignore the real risks.

The design challenge is to choose a few consequential checks, place them at the right moment, and make it normal for anyone to speak up.

slides.title: Protect one vulnerable handoff
slides.html:
Think of a recurring task with an expensive, easily forgotten step: sending an invoice, publishing a release, packing for a trip.

Write a short checklist and use it at the moment of action, not merely when planning. Its value is in preventing a miss, not looking organized.

title: A confusing door is a design problem, not a people problem
hook: If a door looks like it should be pulled but actually needs pushing, who made the mistake?
author: Don Norman
source_title: The Design of Everyday Things (Revised and Expanded Edition)
summary: Don Norman explains how visible cues, natural mappings, and timely feedback let objects communicate how to use them—and why confusing interfaces are often failures of design rather than users.
body: A flat plate on a door suggests pushing. A vertical handle suggests pulling. When the physical cue contradicts the actual action, people make predictable mistakes.
In The Design of Everyday Things, Don Norman describes signifiers, mapping, and feedback as clues that help users understand what actions are possible and what happened afterward.
The practical shift is to stop asking why people fail to understand a product and ask what information the product fails to provide.
takeaways: Make the intended action discoverable before the user acts.
Match controls to outcomes with intuitive mapping.
Give timely feedback so people know whether an action worked.
nuance: Design conventions differ across cultures and contexts. Clear cues reduce confusion but cannot remove every tradeoff or user error.
application: Find a confusing control you use daily. Identify the missing cue, unclear mapping, or absent feedback, then sketch one change.

quiz.question: A door has a handle that invites pulling but only opens by pushing. What is the main design problem?
choices: Users have poor memories
The visible cue suggests the wrong action
The door needs more written instructions
quiz.explanation: The signifier conflicts with the required action, making the mistake predictable.

slides.title: Why did you pull a push door?
slides.html:
You reach for a handle and pull. Nothing happens. A tiny sign says PUSH.

Was that your mistake—or did the door itself invite the wrong action? Don Norman argues that many ordinary frustrations are predictable consequences of how objects communicate.

slides.title: Objects are giving instructions
slides.html:
A flat plate suggests pushing. A graspable handle suggests pulling. These visible hints are signifiers: they tell us where and how to act.

When the hint and the actual mechanism disagree, even attentive people can make the same mistake again and again.

slides.title: Make the next action obvious
slides.html: Good design helps people answer three questions without consulting a manual: What can I do? Which control affects what? Did it work?

items.label: SIGNIFIER
items.title: Where do I act?
items.text: A visible cue points to the action.

slides.title: Spot the missing clue
slides.html: Imagine a stove with four identical knobs arranged in a row, but the burners are arranged in a square. Each knob has a tiny printed label.

interaction.question: What change most directly improves mapping?
choices: Make the labels longer
Arrange the knobs to mirror the burners
Add a louder click when turning a knob
interaction.feedback: Matching the layout of controls to the burners makes their relationship easier to infer.

slides.title: Obvious to whom?
slides.html:
What feels natural depends partly on experience and convention. A gesture familiar to one person may confuse another.

Good design therefore needs observation and testing, not just the designer's intuition. Norman's deeper move is to treat repeated user errors as information about the system.

slides.title: Stop blaming the user
slides.html:
Find one interface that regularly trips people up: a remote, a form, a kitchen control.

Ask whether it hides the possible action, maps controls poorly, or fails to show a result. Then imagine one small change that would prevent the mistake before instructions are needed.

title: The box that rewired world trade
hook: How did an ordinary steel box help reshape where the world makes things?
author: Marc Levinson
source_title: The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger
summary: The shipping container's breakthrough was not just a box: it was a compatible system of ships, trucks, trains, cranes, and ports that made moving goods dramatically easier.
body: In 1956, a converted tanker carried 58 containers from Newark to Houston. The physical box was simple; the system it required was not.
Marc Levinson traces how standard sizes, specialized equipment, investment, and negotiations enabled cargo to move between ships, trains, and trucks without repeatedly unpacking it.
Cheaper, more predictable transport helped reshape manufacturing geography. The lesson is that a modest component can have extraordinary consequences when an entire network becomes compatible.
takeaways: Look for the costly handoffs between otherwise efficient steps.
A standard becomes powerful when many independent participants adopt it.
Infrastructure changes can reorganize markets, jobs, and cities—not just improve one process.
nuance: Containerization was not an overnight or solitary invention. Adoption took years, major capital investment, and labor negotiations; its benefits and disruptions were unevenly distributed.
application: Pick a workflow with repeated handoffs. What shared format or interface would remove re-entry, repacking, or translation between stages?

quiz.question: Why was the shipping container more transformative than a better box alone?
choices: It eliminated the need for ships
It made transport modes work together around a common standard
It made every shipment equally cheap
quiz.explanation: The container's effect depended on interoperable handling across trucks, trains, ships, and ports.

slides.title: A steel box changed the map
slides.html:
In 1956, a converted tanker carried 58 containers from Newark to Houston.

Nothing about a rectangular metal box seems revolutionary. Yet Marc Levinson's The Box shows how this mundane object helped change where factories operate, which ports prosper, and what goods consumers can buy.

slides.title: Every transfer was another job
slides.html:
Before widespread containerization, cargo often had to be handled piece by piece as it moved between transport modes.

Loading, unloading, sorting, and repacking consumed labor and time. The expensive part wasn't always crossing the ocean. It was the messy boundary between one leg of the journey and the next.

slides.title: Make the handoffs disappear
slides.html:
The key was a shared unit that equipment across the transport network could handle.

The breakthrough was interoperability: the box, the cranes, the ships, the trucks, and the ports had to work together.

left.label: Before
left.title: Handle the goods
left.text: Cargo repeatedly unloaded and handled between stages

right.label: After
right.title: Handle the container
right.text: A sealed unit transfers across compatible transport modes

slides.title: A standard needs a coalition
slides.html:
Adoption required expensive port upgrades, new equipment, labor negotiations, and agreement on standards. It took years rather than one brilliant launch.

Once enough of the network became compatible, lower transport costs made distant production more practical—and changed the fortunes of ports and workers.

slides.title: Where is your container?
slides.html:
Imagine a team copying information manually between three tools. Each tool works well on its own.

What would most closely resemble the shipping-container breakthrough?

interaction.prompt: Think of one change that fixes the handoffs, not the individual tools.
interaction.answer: A common data format and reliable import/export interface could let information travel through the whole workflow without repeated manual translation.

slides.title: Small object, large system
slides.html:
Levinson's story is not that a box alone created globalization. It is that a simple standardized component helped coordinate a complicated transport system.

When judging an innovation, ask not only what does this improve? but what other parts of the world can now connect?

title: A perfect map can erase the neighborhood
hook: Why can a beautifully ordered plan fail the people it is meant to help?
author: James C. Scott
source_title: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
summary: James C. Scott argues that sweeping plans often fail when simplified administrative models ignore the local knowledge and relationships that make real communities function.
body: Governments and large organizations need simplified representations to administer complicated places: categories, maps, rules, and measurable targets.
In Seeing Like a State, James C. Scott examines cases where ambitious top-down interventions treated those simplifications as if they were the whole reality, overriding local practices and knowledge.
The practical insight is not to abandon planning. It is to treat a model as a partial view and give affected people a meaningful role in testing and correcting it.
takeaways: Administrative clarity is useful but always selective.
Local practical knowledge can reveal constraints that centralized plans miss.
Test changes with affected people and preserve channels for feedback and revision.
nuance: Scott focuses on particularly consequential failures of authoritarian, high-modernist planning. His argument does not establish that all centralized coordination fails or that local practices are always good.
application: Before standardizing a process, ask people who actually use it what exceptions, workarounds, and dependencies the clean diagram leaves out.

quiz.question: What is the central danger Scott identifies in ambitious top-down planning?
choices: Using any map or metric
Mistaking a simplified administrative view for the full complexity of reality
Consulting local communities too often
quiz.explanation: Simplifications help administration, but treating them as complete can destroy useful local relationships and practices.

slides.title: The plan looks flawless. Then it meets people.
slides.html:
Imagine redesigning a neighborhood from above: straight roads, neat blocks, clear categories. On paper, everything is easier to manage.

But the old neighborhood had informal routes, relationships, and habits invisible on the plan. What happens when the tidy diagram replaces the living place?

slides.title: To govern, you simplify
slides.html:
In Seeing Like a State, James C. Scott examines how powerful institutions make complicated societies easier to describe and administer.

Maps, classifications, and standardized procedures can be genuinely useful. The trouble begins when officials mistake those selective representations for everything that matters.

slides.title: A map is not the neighborhood
slides.html:
A central plan can see roads and official boundaries. Residents may know seasonal shortcuts, informal support networks, and the reasons a seemingly inefficient practice persists.

Neither view is complete on its own.

left.label: From above
left.title: Legible system
left.text: Standard categories, visible routes, measurable outputs

right.label: On the ground
right.title: Lived system
right.text: Tacit know-how, exceptions, relationships, local constraints

slides.title: The missing knowledge has consequences
slides.html:
Scott analyzes large-scale schemes, including forced agricultural and settlement programs, that imposed simplified designs on complex social life.

His concern is especially sharp when confident planners have coercive power and the people affected cannot object, adapt, or reverse the intervention.

slides.title: Would you standardize this?
slides.html:
A company wants every regional team to use exactly the same workflow. The central dashboard shows fewer steps, but local teams report unusual customer needs.

What information should the designers seek before rolling it out?

interaction.prompt: Name a source of knowledge the dashboard probably misses.
interaction.answer: Observe local teams and ask about exceptions, informal workarounds, and downstream effects. Pilot the standard with feedback and a way to revise it.

slides.title: Don't confuse caution with paralysis
slides.html:
Scott is not showing that every large plan is doomed or every local custom is wise.

The narrower, useful warning is about unquestioned simplification plus unchecked power. Good planning needs formal knowledge, local feedback, and room to discover what the model left out.

title: To find your place at sea, bring the time from home
kicker: A clock became a navigation instrument
hook: How can a clock tell a sailor where they are, thousands of miles from shore?
author: Dava Sobel
source_title: Longitude: The True Story of a Lone Genius Who Solved the Greatest Scientific Problem of His Time
summary: Dava Sobel recounts how clockmaker John Harrison helped solve the longitude problem by building timekeepers that could preserve reference time despite the punishing conditions at sea.
body: Latitude was comparatively accessible through celestial observations, but east–west position posed a harder challenge: sailors needed a reliable reference for how far Earth had rotated.
A ship can compare local noon with the time kept at a reference meridian. Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, so one hour of time difference corresponds to 15 degrees of longitude.
John Harrison spent decades building increasingly reliable marine timekeepers. Sobel tells the human story of experimentation, institutional resistance, and the struggle for recognition.
takeaways: A problem that looks geographical may be solved by measuring something else.
A stable reference turns a changing observation into useful information.
Engineering reliability matters as much as a clever principle.
nuance: Marine chronometers were not the only viable longitude method: astronomical lunar-distance techniques also contributed to navigation. Sobel emphasizes Harrison's story, rather than providing a complete history of every solution.
application: When a measurement seems impossible, ask whether a related quantity can be measured reliably and converted into the answer.

quiz.question: Why did keeping accurate reference time help sailors determine longitude?
choices: It directly measured ocean depth
Comparing reference time with local solar time reveals east–west angular difference
It told sailors the latitude without observing the sky
quiz.explanation: Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour. The difference between local solar time and reference time reveals longitude.

slides.title: Lost at sea—with a clock?
slides.html:
Imagine a ship far from land. You can observe the Sun and stars, but how far east or west have you traveled?

For centuries this was a dangerous navigational problem. The unlikely answer was to carry something extraordinarily difficult to keep accurate on a moving ship: time.

slides.title: The Earth is a giant clock
slides.html:
Earth completes one rotation in 24 hours. That means each hour of difference between two locations' solar times corresponds to 15 degrees of longitude.

If you know when it is noon where you are, and what time it is at a reference location, you have the crucial comparison.

slides.title: Compare the Sun with home
slides.html:
Local noon comes from the Sun reaching its highest point. A reference clock preserves the time at a chosen meridian.

The gap between those times reveals east–west position. The idea is simple; making a clock trustworthy through months of ocean travel was not.

left.label: Local observation
left.title: Sun at noon
left.text: What time is it here?

right.label: Reference
right.title: Sea-going clock
right.text: What time is it at the reference meridian?

slides.title: A clockmaker challenged the ocean
slides.html:
Dava Sobel's Longitude follows John Harrison, a self-taught English clockmaker who spent decades refining marine timekeepers.

Movement, temperature changes, and long voyages threatened accuracy. Harrison's achievement was not discovering that time mattered, but making accurate timekeeping practical at sea.

slides.title: What if the Sun is four hours ahead?
slides.html:
Imagine it is local noon on your ship, while your reference clock reads 8 a.m.

Earth rotates 15 degrees each hour. Which way have you traveled from the reference meridian, and roughly how far?

interaction.prompt: Calculate the longitude difference.
interaction.answer: Four hours × 15 degrees = 60 degrees. Local time is ahead of reference time, so the ship is roughly 60 degrees east.

slides.title: Change what you measure
slides.html:
The longitude problem was partly a triumph of reframing: turn a difficult location measurement into a precise time comparison.

There were other navigational solutions, including lunar-distance astronomy. Harrison's story is especially memorable because it shows how much persistent engineering can matter after the core idea is understood.

title: A luxury mushroom grows in the ruins
kicker: What damaged landscapes can still make possible
hook: Why does a prized Japanese delicacy lead an anthropologist into disturbed forests and precarious livelihoods?
author: Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing
source_title: The Mushroom at the End of the World: On the Possibility of Life in Capitalist Ruins
summary: Anna Tsing follows matsutake mushrooms through disturbed forests and global trade to show how ecological relationships and livelihoods persist in landscapes transformed by industrial activity.
body: Matsutake mushrooms can flourish in human-disturbed forests, forming relationships with trees and becoming valuable food in Japan.
Tsing follows the mushroom from foragers and buyers to distant markets, revealing economic activity that depends on complex ecological and social relationships.
Her larger argument challenges the assumption that damaged places are simply empty or finished: life can persist through contingent collaborations, without making destruction desirable.
takeaways: A disturbed ecosystem is not necessarily biologically empty.
Commodity chains depend on relationships that market prices alone do not describe.
Resilience does not erase the harms that made adaptation necessary.
nuance: Tsing offers an ethnographic interpretation, not a controlled test showing that ecological disturbance is beneficial. Matsutake's success in some disturbed forests should not be generalized to other species or ecosystems.
application: When evaluating a damaged system, investigate both what has been lost and which unexpected dependencies, adaptations, or opportunities now exist.

quiz.question: What does matsutake illustrate in Tsing's book?
choices: Environmental damage always improves biodiversity
Ecological and economic life can emerge through complex relationships in disturbed landscapes
All valuable mushrooms can be cultivated industrially
quiz.explanation: The book traces how matsutake, trees, foragers, and markets interact in landscapes shaped by disturbance, without celebrating destruction.

slides.title: A treasure in a damaged forest
slides.html:
Some of the world's most sought-after mushrooms appear in forests shaped by human disturbance.

Matsutake is prized in Japan, yet its story begins in places that might look ruined. Anthropologist Anna Tsing asks what this strange mushroom can reveal about survival, trade, and our assumptions about progress.

slides.title: Life doesn't wait for perfect conditions
slides.html:
Matsutake forms relationships with trees and can thrive in certain disturbed forests. It is not a simple product that growers can reliably manufacture on demand.

Its existence depends on living interactions, forest histories, and conditions that no single actor completely controls.

slides.title: One mushroom, many worlds
slides.html:
Tsing follows matsutake through a network connecting forest ecologies, people who gather mushrooms, traders, and Japanese consumers.

What looks like one expensive product actually rests on several different systems of knowledge and livelihood.

slides.title: The economy isn't only factories
slides.html:
In The Mushroom at the End of the World, Tsing studies a commodity chain that cannot be understood simply as a company designing a product and controlling its production.

Its value emerges from foraging, ecological relationships, cultural preferences, and exchanges across very different communities.

slides.title: What would a price tag miss?
slides.html:
Imagine seeing a costly mushroom in a shop. The price tells you that someone values it—but not how it came to exist.

What would you investigate to understand its real story?

interaction.prompt: Name two relationships hidden behind the price.
interaction.answer: For example, the mushroom's relationship with living trees, the forest's history of disturbance, foragers' local knowledge, or the trading networks connecting distant buyers.

slides.title: Survival is not the same as recovery
slides.html:
Tsing's account is not an argument that damaged forests are better forests. Some organisms find opportunities in disturbed landscapes while others disappear.

The insight is more careful: even amid disruption, unexpected forms of cooperation and survival can persist. Understanding them requires looking closely rather than assuming a place is either pristine or worthless.

title: A safer street needs an audience
kicker: Why an ordinary shop can help a whole block
hook: Could a corner store contribute to street safety simply by giving people a reason to be there?
author: Jane Jacobs
source_title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
summary: Jane Jacobs argued that active sidewalks, street-facing buildings, and everyday watchers help create informal public oversight. A street's safety is shaped not only by formal policing but by the reasons people have to occupy and notice it.
body: Jacobs described how streets with shops and other destinations attract people at different hours, creating a steady presence.
Windows, storefronts, and people on sidewalks provide informal observation: her famous idea of eyes on the street.
The argument is about how urban design supports everyday public life, not a guarantee that busy streets are crime-free.
takeaways: Design reasons for people to use public space, not merely space for them to pass through.
Street-facing activity and repeated casual observation can support informal social oversight.
A lively street and a safe street are related ideas, not identical measures.
nuance: Jacobs's observations and arguments are not a controlled causal estimate of crime reduction. Crowds can also produce risks, and policing, lighting, inequality, and accessibility matter.
application: On your next walk, compare a blank-walled block with one lined by active storefronts. Notice where people linger, where windows face the sidewalk, and which hours leave the street empty.

quiz.question: In Jacobs's account, why can neighborhood shops help street life?
choices: They eliminate the need for any public safety services
They attract people and create opportunities for informal observation
They make every street equally busy at all hours
quiz.explanation: Shops provide destinations and activity; the resulting presence and observation can support informal public oversight.

slides.title: Who watches an ordinary street?
slides.html:
Picture two blocks at dusk. One has a long blank wall. The other has a bakery, a café, and windows overlooking the sidewalk.

Which feels easier to walk through? Jane Jacobs suggested that the answer may have less to do with grand architecture than with everyday people who have reasons to be there.

slides.title: Safety isn't only a uniform
slides.html:
In The Death and Life of Great American Cities, Jacobs described informal oversight by residents, shopkeepers, passersby, and people looking out of windows.

Her phrase eyes on the street captures a simple mechanism: people who use and care about a place can notice what happens there.

slides.title: Design changes who shows up
slides.html:
A sidewalk alone does not guarantee lively public space. The buildings and activities beside it matter.

Places to visit can draw walkers; windows and street-facing entrances connect indoor life to the street.

left.label: Blank edge
left.title: Few reasons to stop
left.text: Long walls, little activity, fewer casual watchers

right.label: Active edge
right.title: Many reasons to visit
right.text: Shops, entrances, windows, people coming and going

slides.title: What would you change first?
slides.html:
A plaza is beautiful but empty after work. Adding another bench might help, but Jacobs would ask a different question.

What regular activity could bring people past the plaza at different hours?

interaction.prompt: Think of one destination and one way to connect it to the street.
interaction.answer: A small evening café, library entrance, or neighborhood service with windows facing the plaza could create reasons to visit and opportunities for casual observation.

slides.title: Busy does not automatically mean safe
slides.html:
Jacobs offered an influential way to observe cities, not a universal formula for preventing crime. Visibility, access, local trust, and formal services all matter.

The practical lesson is to examine what a place invites people to do, rather than judging public space only from its blueprint.

title: When the score becomes the mission
kicker: The hidden cost of measuring everything
hook: What happens when a hospital, school, or company starts optimizing its score rather than the work the score was meant to represent?
author: Jerry Z. Muller
source_title: The Tyranny of Metrics
summary: Jerry Z. Muller argues that performance indicators can become counterproductive when organizations attach rewards and penalties to narrow measurements. Metrics can inform judgment, but should not silently replace it.
body: A measure is a simplified proxy for something we care about, such as learning, patient care, or service quality.
When rewards depend on that proxy, people may concentrate on what is counted and neglect what is harder to measure.
Muller's remedy is not to abandon measurement but to use it alongside informed professional judgment and attention to unintended effects.
takeaways: Ask what a metric omits, not only what it captures.
Tying incentives to a score can change the behavior being measured.
Use multiple sources of evidence and qualitative judgment when stakes are high.
nuance: The book assembles arguments and examples across institutions; it does not establish that every performance metric causes harm. Transparent measurement can reveal failures that intuition misses.
application: Pick one dashboard metric you use. Write down its intended outcome, a way to raise the number without improving that outcome, and one complementary check.

quiz.question: What is the central danger Muller identifies in performance metrics?
choices: Numbers can never represent useful information
A proxy measure can become a target and distort the underlying work
Professional judgment is always more accurate than data
quiz.explanation: When incentives focus on a narrow score, people may improve the score without improving the real objective.

slides.title: The score looks better. Is the work better?
slides.html:
A school celebrates rising test scores. A hospital reports faster patient processing. A company closes more support tickets.

Those numbers may reflect real improvement. But they may also hide a shift toward what is easiest to count. Jerry Muller asks what happens when measurement becomes management's main language.

slides.title: The number is not the goal
slides.html:
A performance metric stands in for a larger outcome. Test scores can represent some learning; ticket counts can represent some productivity.

Neither captures everything. If a reward is attached to the number, people gain a reason to optimize the proxy—even when doing so neglects important work outside it.

slides.title: Two ways to improve a score
slides.html: Consider a customer-support team judged by tickets closed per day. The same dashboard improvement could mean very different things.

left.label: Real gain
left.title: Solve issues faster
left.text: Better tools reduce delays while customers get help

right.label: Metric gain
right.title: Close tickets sooner
right.text: Hard cases are deferred or marked complete too early

slides.title: Measurement changes behavior
slides.html:
In The Tyranny of Metrics, Muller examines education, healthcare, government, and business. His concern is not arithmetic itself but the belief that quantified performance can replace situated judgment.

Public rankings and rewards may amplify gaming, narrow priorities, and pressure to look good rather than do good.

slides.title: Find the missing outcome
slides.html: Imagine a support team celebrates a record number of closed tickets. Before applauding, what would you want to know?

interaction.prompt: Name one complementary measure or observation.
interaction.answer: Check repeat contacts, customer-reported resolution, difficult cases left open, or a sample of conversations. These reveal whether the apparent speed improved actual service.

slides.title: Keep the metric. Keep your judgment.
slides.html:
Measurement can expose hidden problems and challenge biased intuition. Muller does not argue that organizations should stop counting.

Instead, ask whether the number tracks the desired outcome, how incentives might distort it, and which qualitative checks should accompany it. A useful dashboard should support decisions, not make them automatically.
